title: Suburbs and Sprawl
objective: After this level you can explain how cars shaped suburbs.
summary: Suburbs follow transport: ferries, trains, then cars. Postwar highways (1956) and mass-built towns like Levittown spread them. UN-Habitat and Robert Bruegmann disagree about sprawl.

cards.headline: After World War II, a builder made a whole town like a product line.
cards.body: Levittown, New York, built by Levitt and Sons from 1946 to 1951, was an early completely preplanned, mass-produced housing development: more than 17,000 homes. It became a national symbol of suburbia. How do suburbs like it spread so far from the city? Follow the transport.

cards.headline: Suburbs follow the ride
cards.body: Suburbs have always grown along transport. Brooklyn Heights grew after an 1814 ferry to Manhattan; later came trolley-car suburbs, and in London, Level 86's Metro-land along the railway. Each new ride stretched how far from work people could live. After World War II, federal policy and highway construction sped up the growth of American suburbs.

cards.fact: 41,000 miles of new highway, mostly paid by Washington.
cards.context: The Federal-Aid Highway Act, signed on 29 June 1956, authorized 41,000 miles of interstate highways, with the federal government paying 90 percent. A ferry or a train line runs where it runs; a road network reaches much further. Highways were part of the postwar push that sped up the suburbs.

items.label: UN-Habitat
points: Sprawl is driven largely by the car, poor planning and land speculation

items.label: Historian Robert Bruegmann (2005)
points: Sprawl is as old as cities
It gave millions mobility, privacy and choice once reserved for the rich

cards.headline: Suburbs and sprawl: mapped
learned: Suburbs follow transport: ferry, trolley, train, car
Levittown: a mass-produced suburb and a symbol

questions.prompt: Levittown, New York (1946 to 1951) was an early example of what?

options.label: A walled town modeled on medieval European ones
options.rationale: Levittown had no walls; it was a suburb.

options.label: A town built around a new underground railway
options.rationale: It grew in the car era.

options.label: A planned government capital like Washington
options.rationale: It was a private suburb of homes.

questions.explanation: Levittown was an early completely preplanned, mass-produced housing development of more than 17,000 homes.

questions.prompt: In the sprawl debate, which argument did historian Robert Bruegmann make in 2005?

options.label: Sprawl is a brand-new mistake, found only in America
options.rationale: He argued the opposite: it's as old as cities.

options.label: Sprawl brings mobility, privacy and choice once kept for the rich
Sprawl is driven mainly by the car and land speculation
Sprawl should be banned and all suburbs torn down

questions.explanation: Bruegmann argued that sprawl is as old as cities and has given millions mobility, privacy and choice once reserved for the rich; UN-Habitat sees it as car-driven and wasteful of land.

questions.prompt: Level 48 said crowded cities stacked homes into apartments. What let later cities spread homes outward into suburbs?

options.label: Laws that banned apartment buildings
options.rationale: No ban did it; new rides did.

options.label: New transport, from ferries to highways
Cheaper land inside the old city walls
options.rationale: Suburbs grew outward, along the transport.

questions.explanation: Suburbs have always grown along transport: each new ride, from an 1814 ferry to postwar highways, stretched how far from work people could live.
